societies.society: The established leisured Galaxity population under the First Circle

scope.continuity: Bad Dreams album and its described Galaxity background
scope.period: 28th-century Galaxity before Xombul’s Dream Service sabotage
scope.population: Living Galaxity humans receiving continuing technologically supported leisure
exclusions: Film Alpha as an identical economic continuity
Dream users as dead or dormant files
All imperial peripheral workers as similarly leisured

societies.description:
Galaxity’s ordinary residents live after the abolition of work and spend much of their time in technological dream programs. The Dream Service maintains this continuing way of life while a smaller technical and security apparatus remains active. This supports a favorable but cautious guarantee estimate for the central leisured population. The references do not prove that every subject across the wider Terran Empire shares that provision, and external resource labor is not assumed to disappear.

Technocrats of the First Circle govern, and Xombul’s ability to corrupt the Dream Service demonstrates institutional concentration and vulnerability. Control is therefore near concentrated human authority rather than autonomous AI rule: operating a dream system does not make its computer the sovereign. A high, broad nonworking estimate follows the explicit abolition and leisure premise, with allowances for agents, administrators, care and useful creative activity. This is an editorial approximation, not a canonical population census. The point remains comic-specific and does not inherit the film’s different Alpha society or a later economic collapse.

societies.name: Dune — The post-Butlerian Imperium
societies.society: The original novel’s feudal human order under the thinking-machine prohibition

scope.continuity: Frank Herbert original Dune novel/background; later prequels not merged
scope.period: The established Imperium around the opening Arrakis succession crisis
scope.population: Living human Imperial subjects, including laboring populations
exclusions: Later prequel machine-war history as original-novel fact
Every world as an identical welfare system
Film/TV economic changes without separate checks

societies.description:
The Butlerian prohibition excludes thinking machines despite humanity’s known capacity to build them. Trained people such as Mentats fill computational roles, while ordinary non-thinking machinery remains in use. This is a clear technological-restraint zero variant. Its interpretation concerns retained human dependence and useful labor under a religious-political constraint; it does not claim that the Jihad was a modern policy to protect paid jobs.

Great Houses and associated monopolies concentrate authority, placing control near the human-elite position. Guarantees are weak for the broad subject population: security and material access depend heavily on local rulers, caste and place, and Arrakis shows especially harsh subjection and resource control. This is not a fabricated uniform welfare law for every Imperial planet. Real mining, military, administrative, computational and care work remains work. The material does not provide an all-person participation census, so nonworking stays unresolved. The record verifies the book setting without automatically treating every screen adaptation as the same technological and economic order.

guarantees.basis: Known thinking-machine capability is deliberately prohibited while human expertise and labor continue; feudal access and Arrakis subjection weaken guarantees.

control.basis: Great Houses and human institutions control the constrained productive order; ordinary machinery does not become an AI government.

nonworking.basis: Neither the machine prohibition nor Mentat employment provides an all-person useful-work census.
